summary: Updates RFC 5104 to fix the Full Intra Request description for layered codecs: a decoder refresh point must be sent when a FIR arrives on any layer, whether layers use one or several RTP flows.

eli5.summary: When a viewer asks for a fresh full picture, the sender must provide it no matter which layer asked.

questions: what is a full intra request
what is a decoder refresh point
which rtp stream should a fir target
subtitle: A one-paragraph fix that says what a sender must do when a video receiver asks for a fresh full picture on any layer.

tldr.problem: RFC 5104 did not say whether a Full Intra Request (FIR) received for one RTP stream of a layered video bitstream means a refresh for all layers or only for the layer in that stream.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC redefines the decoder refresh point to reset the whole decoder, tells receivers to send FIR on the base layer's stream, and requires a sender to send a refresh point when a FIR arrives on any layer's stream.
tldr.outcome: FIR behavior is now unambiguous for layered codecs. The other payload-specific feedback messages were analyzed and found to need no change.

facts.label: FIR target
facts.value: SSRC of the stream carrying the base layer

today: RFC 8082 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5104. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Problem with FIR and Layers
sections.content:
RFC 4585 and RFC 5104 define payload-specific feedback messages that a media receiver sends as RTCP feedback so a sender can react to what the receiver sees. Since then, layered codecs have become popular. They split the content into sub-bitstreams called layers of different fidelity. Layers can travel in separate RTP streams or be multiplexed into one.

The layers form a pyramid: enhancement layers depend on the base layer and perhaps on other enhancement layers, and the target layer plus everything it depends on must be decoded together. Implementation experience showed that the Full Intra Request (FIR) command of RFC 5104 is underspecified here. When several RTP streams carry one layered bitstream, it was not clear whether a FIR for one stream triggers a decoder refresh point for all layers or only for the layer in that stream.

RFC 8082 updates RFC 5104 to close that gap.
sections.eli5: When a picture is built from stacked sheets, 'start over' was unclear: redo every sheet, or only the one you pointed at? This document settles it.

sections.title: The Updated Decoder Refresh Point
sections.content:
Section 3 replaces the definition of decoder refresh point from RFC 5104 entirely. It is a bit string, packetized in one or more RTP packets, that completely resets the decoder to a known state. A 'hard' refresh point is something like an Intra picture, an IDR picture in H.264 and H.265, or a keyframe in VP8 and VP9. 'Gradual' refresh points are also acceptable, although the user experience usually benefits from a hard one.

A refresh point also carries all the header information above the picture layer that is sent in-band. In H.264 that means the parameter set NAL units needed to decode the following slices, unless the parameter sets were conveyed out of band.

For layered codecs, resetting the decoder to a known state means the refresh point includes hard or gradual single-layer refresh points for all layers. This follows the corresponding definitions in H.264/SVC.
sections.eli5: A refresh point is a clean page that lets the viewer restart from scratch. With layers, the clean page must cover every layer, not just one.

sections.title: How a FIR Works with Layered Codecs
sections.content:
A receiver or middlebox decides when to send a FIR using the guidance in Section 4.3.1 of RFC 5104. When it does, it MUST target the RTP stream that carries the base layer, by setting the SSRC in the Feedback Control Information to the SSRC of the forward RTP stream carrying the base layer.

On the sending side, if a FIR arrives in the RTCP stream associated with any of the RTP streams carrying any layer of the layered bitstream, the designated media sender MUST send a decoder refresh point at its earliest opportunity. Reacting to FIRs tied to enhancement layers is kept for robustness and backward compatibility.

The congestion control requirements of Sections 3.5.1 and 5 of RFC 5104 apply to the forward RTP streams both individually and combined.
sections.eli5: Ask for the restart on the base sheet, the bottom one. But if the sender hears the request about any sheet, it must send a fresh copy of the whole stack as soon as it can.

sections.title: Knowing When Layers Are in Use
sections.content:
This informative section admits that it is surprisingly difficult to tell that a layered bitstream is in use. Implementers are normally expected to know. The risk is with non-pyramid layering, which codecs such as H.264/SVC allow. Applying the new rule blindly there does not break interoperability, but it can cause refresh points to be sent or received where they are not needed, which hurts the user experience.

The negotiated RTP payload format alone is not a reliable indicator, because some layered codecs can form decodable bitstreams from enhancement layers only, without the base layer and without inter-layer prediction. The RFC calls optimized handling of those cases out of scope. A good sign of pyramid-shaped layering is when the RTP streams are bound together in signaling. In SDP, that means they are marked as dependent using the grouping framework of RFC 5888 and the layer dependency signaling of RFC 5583.
sections.eli5: Sometimes it is hard to tell whether sheets really depend on each other. Usually the call setup says so, and that is the best clue.

sections.title: The Other Feedback Messages
sections.content:
RFC 4585 and RFC 5104 define seven payload-specific feedback messages in all. This informative section reviews the six besides FIR and finds no real shortcoming.

  • PLI and SLI: the sensible response is to repair the enhancement layer concerned and the layers depending on it. The encoder can work that out itself, so nothing needs specifying.
  • RPSI and the H.271 VBCM: a missing reference picture reported on any layer must be handled in that layer and all dependent layers. No implementations with layered codecs were known.
  • TSTR/TSTN: the target SSRC may refer to a base layer, an enhancement layer or several layers, so the semantics apply to the layers in the targeted RTP stream. It is unclear whether the sender should adjust bit allocation inside those layers or change the layering structure. The suggestion is to accept TSTR liberally and answer with TSTN indicating 'no change', and for new implementations not to send TSTR except in SRST mode.
sections.eli5: The other kinds of 'please fix this' messages already work fine with layers. Only the 'start over' message needed clearing up.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content: The memo makes no request to IANA. For security, the considerations of RFC 4585 (as updated by RFC 5506) and of RFC 5104 apply, and the clarified response to FIR introduces no additional security considerations.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to register, and no new ways to cause trouble. The old safety rules still apply.
